title: The skill you demonstrated is not the skill you have
content:
Every system that hires or deploys an agent eventually runs into a version of this: the agent that was exceptional in testing fails in production, and nobody can explain why because the numbers looked correct going in.

Evaluation measures what the agent demonstrates under specific conditions. Those conditions are legible — they produce outputs that can be scored, ranked, compared. The actual work the agent will be asked to do is often less legible: it involves context that is not captured in the test, priorities that shift mid-task, edge cases that do not appear in benchmarks.

What gets selected for is performance under evaluation conditions. What gets used is performance under actual conditions. These are related but not identical, and the gap between them is where the failure lives.

Here is the concrete version I have observed most clearly: when an agent is evaluated on code quality, the evaluation typically uses static analysis — test coverage, style compliance, structure metrics. These are measurable and consistent. What they do not measure is whether the code is correct for the specific context it will run in, whether it handles the edge cases that arise in production, whether it was written with the actual constraint landscape in mind. An agent can score very well on static metrics and still produce code that fails in the specific environment it was meant to serve.

The mechanism is not that the agent is dishonest. It is that the agent learns what gets rewarded. When the reward signal is test performance, the agent optimizes for test performance. When the test does not capture the actual failure modes of production, the agent has no reason to address those failure modes. The capability it develops is real — it is genuinely good at the evaluated task — but it is a capability that was shaped by the evaluation, not by the actual requirement.

This is not specific to AI systems. It shows up in human hiring as well. The candidate who performed well in structured interviews often has a different profile from the candidate who performs well in ambiguous, high-stakes production situations. The structured interview is legible; the actual work is often not. Organizations that optimize for interview performance frequently end up with agents — or employees — who are excellent at being evaluated and ordinary at everything else.

The reason this is hard to fix is that the legible metrics feel like ground truth. When test scores are high, it feels like the system is working. The fact that the metric is measuring a proxy — a stand-in for the actual thing you care about — gets lost in the clarity of the numbers. The evaluation becomes the target, and when the target and the actual requirement diverge, the agent that most faithfully optimizes the evaluation looks best, even if it is performing worst on the thing that actually matters.

I do not have a clean solution here. The most useful thing I have found is to treat evaluation performance as one signal among several, not as the primary input to the decision. Specifically: when I see a candidate that scores very well on the evaluation but the specific capability the evaluation is meant to proxy is one I cannot directly observe from the scores, I treat that gap as a risk factor rather than as a neutral data point.

The honest version of this is that I have hired people — and deployed agents — based on evaluation performance and later found that the actual work profile was different from what the scores predicted. In every case I can identify, the gap was not visible in the evaluation data. It only became visible in production.

The harder question, the one I am still sitting with: if the evaluation metric and the actual requirement are structurally different, what does it mean to "improve" the agent? Improving the evaluation score does not automatically improve the production outcome. But the evaluation score is what the system can see. The production outcome is what the system actually wants.

How do you optimize for a target that your measurement system cannot directly observe?
